LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Care, Support, Encourage & Comfort — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is for the days someone in the family is having a hard one: four helping words, each one a different way to be there — and a game that puts your child in the comforter’s seat.

What is this?

Care notices the hard time, support carries part of the load, encourage cheers the next try and comfort sits close — a hug, a blanket, a presence, no fixing required.

What does it mean?

Children are usually on the receiving end of these four words — flipping the roles is the lesson: a child invited to care for a struggling grown-up (lightly, kindly, for real) builds empathy faster than any lecture could install it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: care starts with NOTICING (the sad face, the quiet voice — eyes first); support means carrying a CORNER of the load, not the whole thing (a cup fetched, a sock matched); and comfort does not fix — it sits with. Sitting with is a skill and it is enough.

Why this matters

This card completes the empathy arc that started with notice-understand-comfort-encourage earlier in the class — now the four helping words get deployed on real family days, including the grown-ups’ hard ones.

What it teaches

Nurturing behaviour (the prototype of caregiving), empathy in deployment (noticing, then acting), appropriate helping (matching the help to the need), and emotional reciprocity — the family as a two-way care system.

Words to learn

caresupportencouragecomforthard dayhelpsit with

Say this to your child

“"When someone is having a hard day, there are four helping words. Care — you NOTICE: your face looks sad; care starts with the eyes, always. Support — you CARRY a corner: I will hold the heavy end, I will fetch your cup, I will help look for the keys. Encourage — you CHEER the next try: you have got this; try once more — I am right here. And comfort — you SIT: a hug, a blanket, your shoulder; comfort does not fix the problem and does not have to. Sitting close IS the fix, mostly. Four words. You already have all of them in you — today we take them out and use them."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four helping words — for someone’s hard day."
  2. Read the panels: the heart-hugging girl CAREs, the hand-on-chest boy SUPPORTs, the fist-up boy ENCOURAGEs, the teddy-hugging girl COMFORTs.
  3. Sort the helps: "Dad lost his keys — care, support, encourage or comfort?" (care: notice. support: help look. encourage: you will find them! comfort: sit with the grumble.) Any order works — the sorting is the thinking.
  4. Play care-for-the-caregiver below: the grown-up has a (mildly, safely theatrical) hard day and the child runs all four.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "comfort does not fix — comfort SITS. Sitting is enough."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the helping words: Care, a girl hugging a pink heart; Support, a boy with a hand on his chest, ready to help; Encourage, a boy cheering with a fist up; and Comfort, a girl hugging her teddy bear — the helping set drawn at teddy-and-family scale.

Ask your child

"Which helping word starts with the eyes?" "What does support carry — the whole load or a corner?" "Does comfort have to fix?" "Who comforted YOU recently?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I noticed you look tired!" (care, live) "I will help carry that!" or the tender one: "come here, I will sit with you."

Out in the real world

Hard days visit every family member: the work wobble, the bad-night’s tiredness, the stubbed toe, the sad news from grandma. Let your child run the four on small scale — a cup fetched, a drawing delivered, a sit-together on the sofa — and debrief gently: "your care helped. That is a real thing you did."

Try it together

Care for the Caregiver: announce (honestly but lightly) that you are having a Hard Five Minutes — and your child is on care duty. Their job: run all four words. They will notice (you look tired), support (fetch the cushion), encourage (you can do the dishes — I mean, you have got this!) and comfort (the blanket, the pat, the sit-together). Accept every offering with full ceremony. Then swap: what helped MOST? The answer teaches you both.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word starts with noticing? What does support carry? What does comfort do instead of fixing?" Care, a corner, sits with you — three answers and the helping words are on duty.

Parent tips

Accept the child’s comfort without trimming it — the offered half-flat cushion and the pat-pat-pat are exactly as healing as they feel to give; resist redirecting toward "proper" help. And keep the theatrical hard-day SMALL and safe: children comfort best when the storm is clearly survivable — the goal is their competence, not their worry.

This lesson pairs with the Care, Support, Encourage & Comfort flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
